title.zh: 第一部分 - 安排家庭保险

sections.passage: A telephone conversation between a homeowner, Mrs. Collins, and an insurance agent, David, at Premier Insurance Services. Mrs. Collins has recently purchased a new house and needs to arrange home insurance. David asks her for details about the property. Mrs. Collins explains that the house is a three-bedroom semi-detached property built in 1985, located at 14 Maple Avenue, in the suburb of Northfield. The property has a fitted kitchen, a conservatory, and a detached garage. David asks about the value of the building and its contents. Mrs. Collins estimates the rebuilding cost of the property at 280,000 pounds, based on the surveyor's report she received during the purchase process. She estimates the total value of her household contents at approximately 45,000 pounds, including some valuable items she wants to mention separately: a diamond necklace worth 8,000 pounds, a collection of antique clocks valued at 5,000 pounds, and a laptop computer worth 1,500 pounds. David explains the different levels of cover available. The standard policy costs 35 pounds per month and covers the building and contents against fire, theft, flooding, and storm damage. The premium policy costs 52 pounds per month and adds accidental damage cover, legal expenses protection, and emergency home assistance. David recommends the premium policy because Mrs. Collins's house is in an area that has a moderate flood risk rating. Mrs. Collins asks about the excess, and David explains that the standard excess is 250 pounds per claim, but this can be reduced to 100 pounds by paying an additional 5 pounds per month. Mrs. Collins also asks about discounts, and David tells her that installing a burglar alarm gives a 10 percent discount, and having smoke detectors on every floor gives an additional 5 percent discount. Mrs. Collins confirms that the house has both, so she qualifies for a 15 percent discount on her premium. She decides to go with the premium policy and provides her bank details for monthly direct debit payments.

title.en: Section 2 - Presentation about a New Sports Centre
title.zh: 第二部分 - 关于新体育中心的介绍

sections.passage: Good morning, and thank you all for attending this presentation about the new Riverside Sports and Leisure Centre, which will open its doors to the public on the 1st of March. I'm Simon Blake, the project manager, and I'm excited to share with you what this fantastic new facility has to offer. The centre is located on the banks of the River Trent, adjacent to the existing Riverside Park, and covers a total area of 12,000 square metres. It has been built at a cost of 18 million pounds, funded jointly by the local council and a grant from Sport England. The main building houses a 50-metre Olympic-standard swimming pool, a 25-metre teaching pool, and a leisure pool with water slides and a wave machine. The swimming pools will be open from 6 AM to 10 PM on weekdays and from 7 AM to 8 PM on weekends. In addition to the aquatic facilities, the centre has a large multi-sports hall that can accommodate basketball, badminton, volleyball, and indoor football. There is also a state-of-the-art gymnasium equipped with over 150 pieces of fitness equipment, including cardio machines, free weights, and functional training areas. The gym will offer free induction sessions for all new members, conducted by our team of qualified fitness instructors. For younger visitors, we have a dedicated children's soft play area and a crèche facility that is available for children aged 6 months to 5 years while parents use the gym or attend classes. The crèche costs 4 pounds per hour per child and can be booked in advance online. Outside, the centre features four outdoor tennis courts, a full-size artificial turf football pitch, and a 2-kilometre cycling and running track along the river. Membership options include a monthly fee of 45 pounds for adults, 25 pounds for students and seniors, and a family membership for 85 pounds per month covering two adults and up to three children. There is also a pay-as-you-go option for non-members. The centre will host an open day on the 23rd of February, where the public can tour the facilities and try sample classes free of charge.

title.en: Section 3 - Discussion about a Science Presentation
title.zh: 第三部分 - 关于科学报告的讨论

sections.passage: Two students, Nathan and Hannah, are preparing a presentation for their Environmental Science module. They need to present their research on the effectiveness of different renewable energy technologies in reducing carbon emissions. Nathan has been researching solar energy and wind power, while Hannah has focused on hydroelectric and tidal energy. Nathan begins by sharing his findings on solar power. He has discovered that global solar capacity has grown enormously in the past decade, increasing from about 40 gigawatts in 2010 to over 700 gigawatts in 2022. The cost of solar panels has dropped by approximately 90 percent since 2010, making solar energy competitive with fossil fuels in many regions. However, Nathan points out that solar energy has limitations, including intermittency — solar panels only generate electricity during daylight hours — and the large land area required for solar farms. Hannah presents her research on tidal energy, which she finds particularly interesting because it is highly predictable, unlike wind and solar. Tides follow regular cycles that can be forecast years in advance, making tidal energy a reliable source of renewable power. However, she notes that tidal energy technology is still in its early stages, and there are currently only a few operational tidal power stations worldwide. The largest is the Sihwa Lake Tidal Power Station in South Korea, which has a capacity of 254 megawatts. The environmental impact of tidal barrages on marine ecosystems is also a concern. They discuss how to structure their presentation. Their tutor, Dr. Foster, has asked each group to include a section on the economic viability of their chosen technologies. Nathan has found that the levelized cost of solar energy has fallen to around 40 dollars per megawatt hour, making it one of the cheapest sources of electricity. Hannah has data showing that tidal energy is currently much more expensive, at around 300 dollars per megawatt hour, but that costs are expected to decrease as the technology matures. They decide to create a comparison table for their slides showing the cost, predictability, environmental impact, and scalability of each technology. They agree to meet on Thursday evening to finalize their presentation, which they will deliver the following Monday. Dr. Foster has allocated 15 minutes for each group's presentation plus 5 minutes for questions.

title.en: Section 4 - Lecture on the History of Public Health
title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于公共卫生历史的讲座

sections.passage: Good morning. Today's lecture traces the history of public health from its earliest beginnings to the modern era. Public health, defined as the organized efforts of society to prevent disease, promote health, and prolong life, has been one of the most significant contributors to the dramatic increase in human life expectancy over the past two centuries. In the early 19th century, the average life expectancy in industrialized countries was approximately 40 years. Today, it exceeds 80 years in most developed nations, and public health measures deserve much of the credit for this extraordinary improvement. The modern public health movement began in the 1840s with the work of Edwin Chadwick in England. Chadwick's landmark report, published in 1842, documented the appalling living conditions of the urban poor and demonstrated a clear link between poverty, unsanitary conditions, and disease. His work was instrumental in passing the Public Health Act of 1848, which established a Central Board of Health and gave local authorities the power to improve sanitation and drainage. Perhaps the most important figure in the early history of public health was John Snow, a London physician who is widely regarded as the father of epidemiology. During the cholera epidemic of 1854, Snow meticulously mapped the locations of cholera cases in the Soho district of London and traced the outbreak to a contaminated water pump on Broad Street. By removing the handle of the pump, he effectively ended the epidemic. His work demonstrated for the first time that cholera was a waterborne disease, challenging the prevailing miasma theory which held that diseases were caused by bad air. The late 19th and early 20th centuries saw the development of vaccination programmes that would save millions of lives. Following Edward Jenner's pioneering smallpox vaccine of 1796, vaccination campaigns gradually expanded to cover other diseases. By the mid-20th century, vaccines were available for diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, and measles. The World Health Organization's successful campaign to eradicate smallpox, declared complete in 1980, remains the greatest achievement of global public health. The discovery of antibiotics, beginning with Alexander Fleming's accidental discovery of penicillin in 1928, revolutionized the treatment of bacterial infections and saved countless lives. However, the growing problem of antibiotic resistance now threatens to undo much of this progress. The World Health Organization has identified antimicrobial resistance as one of the top ten global public health threats, warning that common infections could once again become lethal if antibiotics lose their effectiveness. In the 21st century, public health faces new challenges, including the global rise of non-communicable diseases such as diabetes, heart disease, and obesity, the mental health crisis, and the threat of future pandemics. The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated both the power of modern public health tools — including rapid vaccine development and genomic surveillance — and the devastating consequences when public health systems are inadequate or when scientific guidance is ignored. As we look to the future, the lessons of public health history remind us that investment in prevention, research, and equitable access to healthcare can achieve remarkable results.

sections.passage:
Coffee is one of the world's most popular beverages, with over 2.25 billion cups consumed every day. Its journey from an obscure plant in the highlands of Ethiopia to a global commodity worth over 100 billion dollars annually is a remarkable story of cultural transformation, economic ambition, and colonial expansion.

According to Ethiopian legend, coffee was discovered by a goat herder named Kaldi in the 9th century. Kaldi noticed that his goats became unusually energetic after eating the red berries from a particular tree. He tried the berries himself and experienced a similar burst of vitality. Word of the miraculous berries spread, and monks at a nearby monastery began using them to stay awake during long hours of prayer. Whether or not this story is true, it is generally accepted that the coffee plant, Coffea arabica, originated in the forests of the Ethiopian highlands.

By the 15th century, coffee drinking had spread throughout the Arabian Peninsula. The city of Mocha in present-day Yemen became the first major centre of the coffee trade, and the port lent its name to a variety of coffee that remains popular today. Coffee houses, known as qahveh khaneh, sprang up in cities across the Ottoman Empire and quickly became important centres of social and political life. Patrons gathered to drink coffee, play chess, discuss politics, and listen to music. The Ottoman authorities recognized the social importance of coffee houses and at various times attempted to ban them, fearing that they were breeding grounds for political dissent.

Coffee reached Europe in the 17th century through Venetian traders and quickly gained popularity despite initial resistance from some quarters. The Catholic Church initially condemned coffee as the drink of the infidels, but Pope Clement VIII reportedly tasted it and, enjoying the flavour, gave it his approval. Coffee houses proliferated across Europe, becoming centres of intellectual exchange. In London, establishments such as Lloyd's Coffee House, which opened in 1686, evolved into important financial institutions — Lloyd's of London, the world's leading insurance market, began as a coffee house where maritime insurance was arranged.

The European demand for coffee drove the establishment of coffee plantations in tropical colonies, often using enslaved labour. The Dutch established coffee cultivation in Java in the 1690s, and the French introduced it to the Caribbean in the 18th century. Brazil, which received coffee seedlings in the 1720s, would eventually become the world's largest producer, a position it still holds today. The colonial coffee trade was built on the exploitation of millions of enslaved Africans and indigenous peoples, a legacy that continues to affect the global coffee industry. Today, the global coffee industry employs an estimated 125 million people worldwide, with the majority of production concentrated in developing countries. However, many coffee farmers receive only a tiny fraction of the retail price of their product, and volatile market prices make it difficult for smallholder farmers to earn a sustainable living. Fairtrade certification and direct trade relationships have emerged as attempts to address these inequalities, though their impact remains debated.

title.en: Passage 2 - The Benefits and Risks of Bilingualism
title.zh: 文章2 - 双语的利与弊

sections.passage:
More than half of the world's population speaks at least two languages, making bilingualism the norm rather than the exception. Yet for much of the 20th century, researchers believed that bilingualism was a disadvantage, particularly for children, who they thought would be confused by learning two languages simultaneously. Modern neuroscience has comprehensively overturned this view, revealing that bilingualism confers significant cognitive, social, and even economic advantages, though it is not without certain costs.

The cognitive benefits of bilingualism have been extensively documented. Research by Professor Ellen Bialystok at York University in Toronto has shown that bilingual individuals consistently outperform monolinguals on tasks that require executive function — the set of mental processes that includes attention control, cognitive flexibility, and the ability to switch between tasks. This advantage appears to stem from the constant exercise that bilingual brains get from managing two language systems. Every time a bilingual person speaks, their brain must select the appropriate language while suppressing the other, a process that strengthens the neural networks responsible for executive control.

Perhaps most remarkably, bilingualism appears to provide some protection against age-related cognitive decline. A landmark study published in the journal Neurology in 2013, which followed 648 patients with dementia, found that bilingual patients developed symptoms of dementia an average of 4.5 years later than monolingual patients, even though both groups showed the same level of brain damage on brain scans. This suggests that bilingualism does not prevent the underlying pathology of dementia but rather enables the brain to compensate for it more effectively, a concept known as cognitive reserve.

The social benefits of bilingualism are equally significant. Bilingual individuals have access to wider social networks and can communicate with a larger and more diverse range of people. They also tend to demonstrate greater cultural sensitivity and empathy. Research has shown that bilingual children are better at understanding other people's perspectives, a skill known as theory of mind. This may be because bilingual children regularly experience situations where different people speak different languages, requiring them to consider what others know and do not know about language.

However, bilingualism is not without its challenges. Bilingual individuals typically have a smaller vocabulary in each individual language compared to monolingual speakers of those languages, though their combined vocabulary across both languages is usually larger. They may also experience more frequent tip-of-the-tongue moments — the frustrating sensation of knowing a word but being unable to retrieve it. Some bilingual speakers report that they feel less emotionally connected to their second language, preferring to express strong emotions or intimate thoughts in their first language.

The economic benefits of bilingualism are increasingly recognized in our globalized world. A study by The Economist estimated that the ability to speak a second language can increase lifetime earnings by an average of 50,000 dollars or more, depending on the language and the industry. In the European Union, where 24 official languages are spoken, multilingualism is actively promoted as an economic asset. Companies with multilingual employees can access new markets, negotiate more effectively with international partners, and better serve diverse customer bases.

title.en: Passage 3 - The Future of Food Production
title.zh: 文章3 - 食品生产的未来

sections.passage:
Feeding a global population projected to reach nearly 10 billion by 2050 is one of the most pressing challenges facing humanity. Current food production systems are already under enormous strain, contributing to approximately 25 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, consuming 70 percent of the world's freshwater, and occupying nearly 40 percent of the Earth's ice-free land surface. Finding ways to produce more food while reducing environmental impact is therefore one of the defining challenges of the 21st century.

One of the most promising developments is precision agriculture, which uses technology to optimize farming practices at a granular level. GPS-guided tractors can plant seeds with centimetre-level accuracy, drones equipped with multispectral cameras can detect crop diseases before they become visible to the naked eye, and soil sensors can measure moisture and nutrient levels in real time. By applying water, fertilizers, and pesticides only where and when they are needed, precision agriculture can reduce input costs by up to 30 percent while maintaining or increasing yields. A study by the University of Cambridge found that farms using precision agriculture techniques reduced their nitrogen fertilizer use by 20 percent without any loss in crop productivity.

Gene editing technologies, particularly CRISPR-Cas9, offer another avenue for improving food production. Unlike traditional genetic modification, which involves introducing foreign DNA into an organism, CRISPR allows scientists to make precise changes to an organism's existing genetic code. This technology has been used to develop crop varieties that are more resistant to drought, disease, and pests. In 2021, researchers at the University of Tokyo used CRISPR to develop a tomato variety that produces five times more of a substance called GABA, which has been shown to help lower blood pressure. Gene-edited crops are subject to varying levels of regulation around the world, with the United States and Japan generally taking a more permissive approach than the European Union.

Vertical farming, which involves growing crops in stacked layers within controlled indoor environments, is another rapidly growing field. Vertical farms can operate year-round regardless of weather conditions, produce crops using up to 95 percent less water than conventional farming, and eliminate the need for pesticides. A single vertical farm the size of a large warehouse can produce as much lettuce as a 40-hectare outdoor farm. However, vertical farming currently has significant limitations. The high energy costs associated with artificial lighting make it economically viable only for high-value crops such as leafy greens and herbs. Staple crops like wheat, rice, and corn, which require far more energy to grow and constitute the bulk of global calorie consumption, are not currently practical to grow in vertical farms.

Perhaps the most radical innovation is the development of cultured meat — meat grown from animal cells in a laboratory rather than obtained from slaughtered animals. Companies such as Upside Foods and GOOD Meat have received regulatory approval to sell cultured chicken in the United States and Singapore. Proponents argue that cultured meat could dramatically reduce the environmental footprint of meat production, using up to 96 percent less water, 99 percent less land, and producing 96 percent fewer greenhouse gas emissions than conventional beef production. However, the technology remains extremely expensive, and scaling production to levels that could meaningfully replace conventional meat remains a formidable engineering challenge.

options.en: They do not grow well indoors
High energy costs make them uneconomical
options.zh: 高能源成本使它们不经济
消费者更喜欢户外种植的主粮

text.en: What is cultured meat?
text.zh: 什么是培养肉？

options.en: Meat from animals raised on organic farms
options.zh: 有机农场饲养的动物肉

options.en: Meat grown from animal cells in a laboratory
options.zh: 在实验室中从动物细胞培养的肉
使用传统方法保存的肉

text.en: How much less water does cultured beef use compared to conventional beef?
text.zh: 培养牛肉比传统牛肉少用多少水？

text.en: Which countries have approved cultured meat for sale?
text.zh: 哪些国家已批准培养肉销售？

text.en: What is the main barrier to cultured meat production?
text.zh: 培养肉生产的主要障碍是什么？

text.en: How much less land does cultured beef use compared to conventional?
text.zh: 培养牛肉比传统牛肉少用多少土地？

text.en: What advantage do vertical farms have over outdoor farming?
text.zh: 垂直农场比户外农业有什么优势？

options.zh: 全年运营不受天气影响

options.en: No need for any energy input

text.en: Which regions take a more permissive approach to gene-edited crops?
text.zh: 哪些地区对基因编辑作物采取更宽容的态度？

prompt.en: The pie charts below show the main reasons why students chose a particular university in two different years, 2010 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
prompt.zh: 下面的饼图显示了2010年和2020年学生选择某所大学的主要原因。通过选择和报告主要特征来总结信息，并在相关地方进行比较。至少写150个单词。

prompt.en: Some people think that technology has made our lives more complicated rather than simpler. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
prompt.zh: 一些人认为技术使我们的生活变得更复杂而非更简单。你在多大程度上同意或不同意？给出你回答的理由，并包括你自己的知识或经验中任何相关的例子。至少写250个单词。
